idiom_name: hand-written `impl Trait for Wrapper` forwarders (Deref as the transparent special case)
implementation_notes: Rust has no inheritance to replace and no stable delegation syntax: the wrapper owns or borrows the delegate in a field and every trait method to be reused is written out as a forwarder in `impl Trait for Wrapper`, forwarding the borrow (`&self`) or the field (`&mut self`). The compiler checks completeness, so a forgotten trait method is a compile error rather than a silent hole - the main advantage over reflective languages. `Deref`/`DerefMut` is the one mechanism that forwards without writing the members: implement it and method resolution transparently reaches the target, but the standard library itself warns that this exposes the whole target API and should only be done when the type transparently behaves like the target. The `reuse` keyword (RFC 3530, `fn_delegation`) is still an unstable feature, so the `delegate` macro is the practical way to remove the boilerplate today.
pitfalls: Trait impls are checked, inherent methods are not: a method you forget to forward is simply absent, and a name that collides with one of the wrapper's own methods silently wins at the call site (method resolution prefers inherent methods before Deref).

`Deref`-based forwarding ships the entire target API and is discouraged for anything that is not smart-pointer-like; with a generic `Deref` impl every method name risks colliding with the wrapper's own.

Borrow checking makes mutable forwarding explicit - forwarding `&mut self` methods while the wrapper also reads its own state needs split borrows - and re-entrant delegation through a shared delegate behind a lock can deadlock.

variants.name: Macro-generated forwarders (delegate!/ambassador)
variants.idiom_name: `delegate! { to self.inner { fn push(&mut self, v: u32); } }`
variants.implementation_notes: The `delegate` crate writes the forwarders from a declaration: name the target expression, list the methods, and the macro expands to the same `impl` you would hand-write, with attributes for renaming (`#[call(len)]`), argument conversion (`#[into]`), `#[await]`, field access and enum-variant delegation. It removes the maintenance burden of keeping signatures in sync, at the cost of restating the signatures in the macro (Rust cannot enumerate a trait's methods without reflection - the RFC 3530 discussion says this explicitly) and of a proc-macro dependency in the build. Use it for wrappers over wide traits; hand-write when only one or two methods are forwarded.
pitfalls: Every signature is still restated (no reflection), so trait changes still require edits - they are just gathered into one block instead of spread across methods.
Macro expansion hides the forwarder from IDE navigation: the wrapper appears to have no such method, and `#[call(...)]`/`#[into]` mistakes surface as errors inside expanded code.
The crate inserts `#[inline(always)]` on generated forwarders, which can bloat hot generic code - declare `#[inline]` yourself to override that choice.
